Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me).

TASK: build the content pipeline for Kodely's SEO pages, and seed it with a first batch of genuinely accurate articles.

## Context
There is a `BlogPost` model in `prisma/schema.prisma` (READ ONLY) with: slug, title, metaDescription, category, targetKeyword, bodyHtml, publishedAt, updatedAt. `app/blog/` and `app/blog/[slug]/` already exist — read them first to see how posts are rendered and what shape `bodyHtml` is expected to be. There is also `seo-batch1.json` in the repo root worth reading for prior art on the intended format.

## THE HARD CONSTRAINT — read this twice
The project's planning board contains roughly 250 SEO article briefs, and **a large number of them describe features Kodely does not have.** Publishing an article that says Kodely does something it cannot is (a) a lie to a prospective customer, (b) an immediate bounce when they sign up and it isn't there, and (c) a refund request.

So: **before writing a single sentence about a capability, verify it in the code.** Ground truth lives in:
- `lib/agent.ts` — the SYSTEM prompt. This is the definitive statement of what generated sites can and cannot contain. Read it in full.
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the exact starting project and its dependencies.
- `lib/build-site.ts` — how sites are compiled.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/**` — how published sites are served, and the CSP they run under.
- `lib/credits.ts` — how pricing/credits actually work.
- `app/api/projects/[id]/export/route.ts`, `app/api/enhance/route.ts`, `lib/assets/` — recently added capabilities.

Things I already know are TRUE and are strong, honest angles: generated sites are real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind apps (not HTML mockups); you are never charged for a build that fails to compile; you can export your full source as a zip; sites are compiled server-side and served static.

Things I know are FALSE right now — do NOT claim any of them: databases or any backend, user accounts/auth on generated sites, working contact forms that deliver mail, e-commerce/checkout, external API integrations, stock photography or remote images of any kind, custom web fonts, multi-page routing (it is a single-page app), or npm packages beyond react/react-dom.

If a topic cannot be written honestly, **do not write it** — list it in your report as "cannot be written truthfully until X ships". That list is genuinely valuable output; a short honest batch beats a long dishonest one.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `scripts/seo/` AND `content/seo/`
Do NOT edit `app/blog/**` — read it to learn the render contract, but another agent may be in that area. Write your articles as data files plus a seeding script.

## What to build
1. **A seed script** (`scripts/seo/seed.mjs`) that upserts articles into the `BlogPost` table by slug — idempotent, safe to re-run, and with a `--dry-run` that prints what would change without writing. Load `.env` yourself for DATABASE_URL.
2. **10-15 genuinely accurate articles** as structured data files. Prioritise honest, high-intent topics: comparisons where you can only speak factually about Kodely's own side, "how to build X" guides where X is actually buildable (a restaurant landing page, a portfolio, a barber shop site), and explainers about how AI site generation works.
3. **A validator** (`scripts/seo/validate.mjs`) checking every article for: unique slug, title length under ~60 chars, metaDescription 50-160 chars, valid HTML that matches what `app/blog/[slug]` expects, no unclosed tags, and no external resource references.

## Writing standards
- `bodyHtml` is pre-rendered semantic HTML — check how `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx` renders it and match exactly what it expects.
- Write for a real person deciding whether to use this, not for a keyword crawler. No "In today's digital landscape". No padding to hit a word count.
- Do not invent statistics, customer counts, testimonials, review scores, or awards. If you want a number, it must come from the code (e.g. actual credit costs from lib/credits.ts) — and read `SIGNUP_GRANT` and the `estimateCredits` comments carefully, because the real per-build cost is currently uncertain and being re-measured. Prefer not quoting a specific price at all over quoting one that will be wrong next week.
- When naming competitors, state only verifiable, non-disparaging facts, and prefer describing Kodely's own behaviour over characterising theirs.

## Critical constraints
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies.
- DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint <your files>`; your files must be clean.
- You may run your seed script against the local database in `--dry-run` mode freely. Only do a real write if you are confident it is idempotent, and do not delete rows you did not create.

## Report back
The articles you wrote and the specific code file that grounds each capability claim, the list of board topics that CANNOT be written truthfully today and what would need to ship first, and anything you found in the existing blog rendering that constrains the format.

{ "slug": "how-ai-website-builders-actually-work", "title": "How AI Website Builders Actually Work", "metaDescription": "What happens between typing a description and seeing a website: the agent, the tools it has, the compile step, and where it can go wrong.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "how ai website builders work", "body": [ "

", "

Step 1: your project starts from a real foundation, not a blank page

", "

Before the model sees anything, the project already exists. A new Kodely project is a working Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind app: a package.json, a Vite config, a tsconfig, an index.html, an entry point, a stylesheet, an App.tsx, and a handful of UI primitives — a Button, a Card, a Section, a Nav.

", "

This matters more than it sounds. The model is never asked to invent a build system, and it can't pick dependencies — the foundation's package.json is the only dependency set that will ever exist, and it's just React and React DOM. Fewer degrees of freedom means far fewer ways for the output to be broken.

", "

Step 2: the model gets tools, not a text box

", "

The generation step isn't \"write me some HTML\". The model runs as an agent with exactly two tools: write a file, and delete a file. It's given the current contents of every source file in your project plus your request, and it works by writing complete files back.

", "

There's no patch or diff tool — every write is the whole final file. That's a deliberate trade: patches are smaller but they fail in subtle, hard-to-detect ways when the model's mental model of the file has drifted. A complete file either parses or it doesn't.

", "

Every path the model asks to write is normalised and checked before anything touches the database. Absolute paths, backslashes, and anything containing .. are rejected outright, so a confused model can't write outside its own project.

", "

Step 3: the site gets compiled — for real

", "

This is the step that separates a website from a plausible-looking pile of text. Once the model has finished writing files, Kodely runs an actual production build of your project on the server: TypeScript and JSX compiled, Tailwind processed, the bundle emitted.

", "

", "

The build runs in a throwaway directory with a fixed 60-second ceiling, against a pre-installed copy of the foundation's dependencies. There is no npm install per generation, which is both why it's fast and why the model can't introduce a package.

", "

Step 4: if it didn't compile, it gets one repair attempt

", "

When the build fails, the compiler error goes straight back to the model with the instruction to fix it and keep the rest of the change. It gets one such attempt. If the second build also fails, the whole generation is marked failed.

", "

A failed build costs you zero credits. That rule is in the billing code, not just in the marketing copy: the charge only ever happens on the success path. ", "

A successful build's compiled output is what you see in the preview pane, and it's the same output that gets published. You're not previewing an approximation of the site — you're looking at the built artefact.

", "

Publishing copies that compiled output to the published tree and serves it at a kodely.site subdomain as static files. Before it goes live, the files are scanned for anything that looks like a real API key or secret, and the publish is blocked if one turns up.

", "

The sandbox is the shape of the product

", "

That's a real limitation and it's worth understanding rather than discovering. It also removes an entire category of quiet breakage — nothing on your published page can stop working because someone else's CDN went down or changed a URL. The full reasoning is here.

", "

What the model is and isn't deciding

", "

People assume the AI is making infrastructure decisions. It isn't. It doesn't choose a framework, a hosting provider, a database, or a package. Those were decided once, in the foundation, by people. The model's job is narrower and more like a designer's: structure, layout, components, copy, colour, type.

", "

Narrow is the point. Most of the horror stories about AI-generated code come from agents given wide latitude over systems they can't verify. An agent that can only edit React components in a project that gets compiled and type-checked every single time has a very small blast radius.

", "

Where it genuinely goes wrong

", "
  • Vague prompts. The model fills gaps with the average of everything it has seen, which reads as generic. Specificity is the fix.

The short version

Fixed foundation, agent with two file tools, real server-side compile, one repair attempt, zero charge on failure, static publish under a locked-down policy. No magic anywhere in the chain — just a narrow job, done in a place where being wrong is caught immediately.

Here is the exact technical reason, and how to design around it.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai website builder no images", "body": [ "

If you build a site with Kodely, it will contain no photographs. Not stock photos, not AI-generated photos, not images pulled from anywhere else. This is the limitation people notice first, so here's the actual reason and what to do about it — rather than a paragraph explaining that constraints are secretly good for you.

The reason, precisely

Every published Kodely site is served under a strict content security policy. In effect it says: this page may load resources from itself, and images may additionally be inline data. Requests to any other origin are blocked, and the page's ability to make network requests at all is switched off.

", "

", "

The builder is told about this constraint directly, so it doesn't write markup that would fail. That's why you don't get a broken-image icon: you get a design that never asked for the image in the first place.

", "

Why the policy is that strict

", "

Kodely takes text from anyone on the internet, turns it into code with a language model, compiles it, and serves it from a domain we own. If those pages could load and execute code from arbitrary third-party hosts, that pipeline becomes a very convenient way to host something malicious with our name on the certificate.

", "

Blocking all external requests removes that entire category at once. It also means a published site can't quietly break later because somebody else's CDN moved a URL, changed their terms, or went down. A Kodely site has no third-party dependencies at runtime, which is an unusual and genuinely nice property for a small business page.

", "

The honest accounting: you lose photography, and you gain a page that can't be turned into an attack surface and can't rot from the outside.

Everything visual is drawn by the page itself:

  • CSS gradients and colour. Layered gradients and mesh-style backgrounds carry a surprising amount of a design's atmosphere, and they scale to any screen size with no image at all.
  • Typography and space. With no photograph to lean on, type size, weight, colour and generous white space have to do the work — which tends to push a design towards being deliberate rather than decorated.
  • System fonts. The system stack, not a custom web font. More on that below.
", "

The font part, since it surprises people

You can't use a custom web font either, and not just remotely-hosted ones — a font embedded as a base64 data URI is also blocked. The policy allows data URIs for images but not for other resource types, and fonts fall into the second category. So a base64 font fails exactly like a remote one.

", "

Sites use the system font stack instead — the same one most operating systems use for their own interface. It's a real constraint on brand expression. It's also the fastest possible text rendering, with no layout shift while a font loads.

What we're not going to do

Here is exactly what Kodely does when that happens, why you are not charged, and what to try next.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai website builder build failed", "body": [ "

Language models write code that doesn't compile. Not often, but often enough that how a builder handles it is a real product decision rather than an edge case. Here's precisely what Kodely does, and what you should do on your side.

", "

Failure means something specific here

", "

Every Kodely generation ends with a real production build of your project on our servers — TypeScript and JSX compiled, Tailwind processed, a bundle emitted. \"Failed\" means that build returned a non-zero exit code: a type error, an unclosed tag, a missing import, a typo'd prop, a syntax error.

", "

This is a stricter and more useful definition than most builders use. A tool that generates raw HTML has almost nothing that can fail — the page will render something no matter how wrong it is, and you find the problem yourself, later, in a browser. Compiling means a whole class of mistakes gets caught by a machine before you ever see the page.

", "

The first thing that happens: one repair attempt

", "

When the build fails, Kodely doesn't hand you the error. It sends the compiler output straight back to the model with the instruction to fix it and keep the rest of the change intact, then builds again.

", "

You'll see the status change to say the build didn't compile and is being fixed. In most cases the second build succeeds and the whole episode is twenty extra seconds you barely notice.

", "

There is exactly one repair attempt. If the second build also fails, the generation stops and is marked failed. That ceiling is deliberate — it bounds the worst case at roughly twice a normal generation instead of an open-ended loop, and a model that couldn't fix its own error twice is unlikely to fix it on the seventh attempt.

", "

You are not charged

", "

A failed build costs zero credits. Not a discount, not a partial charge — zero.

", "

This is enforced structurally rather than by policy. Credits are only ever deducted on the success path of a build; the failure path writes a record of the build with its true measured cost and a charge of zero. There is no code path where a failed build takes credits from your balance, which means it can't be quietly changed by someone adjusting a setting.

", "

Worth being clear about what this does and doesn't cover: the model tokens spent on a failed build are real money that Kodely pays and you don't. That's a cost we absorb precisely because \"you paid for something broken\" is the single worst experience this category has to offer. The repair attempt is capped at one partly to keep that promise affordable to keep.

", "

What you'll see

", "

An error message with the reason, your credit balance unchanged, and your project exactly as it was. Your previous working version is untouched — a failed generation doesn't leave you with a half-broken site.

", "

If your browser tab closes or your connection drops mid-generation, the in-flight model request is actually cancelled rather than left running to completion for nobody. That build is recorded as failed and, again, charged nothing.

", "

What to do next

", "

Failures cluster around a few causes, and the fix is different for each.

", "

  • It was just bad luck. Sometimes it is. Re-running the same prompt is a perfectly reasonable response, and it costs you nothing if it fails again.
", "

Rolling back is always available and always free

", "

Separately from failures: every successful build is saved as a checkpoint under the History tab. If a build succeeds but you don't like the result, you can restore any earlier checkpoint.

", "

Rolling back costs nothing. It isn't a generation — it restores a snapshot of files you already paid for when that build ran, including the already-compiled output, so the preview is correct immediately and there's no rebuild that could itself fail. That makes an ambitious edit a cheap experiment rather than a gamble.

", "

Why we talk about this at all

Most tools in this category would rather not mention that generation fails. But everyone who uses one finds out within a week, and the thing that determines whether they stay isn't whether it ever fails — it's whether failing cost them anything.

", "

Decide the one action first

", "

Before you write a prompt, finish this sentence: this page succeeds if the visitor ___. Joins the waitlist. Books a call. Downloads the thing. Buys. Calls you.

", "

Pages fail when the answer is \"learns about us\", because that isn't an action and nothing on the page can be designed to produce it. One action, named, decides your headline, your sections and where the buttons go.

", "

The structure that works

", "
  1. Headline. What it is and who it's for, in a sentence a stranger understands. Not a slogan.
  2. Subhead. The specific promise, plus who it isn't for. Naming who it's not for makes the rest more believable.
  3. The action, immediately. Above the fold, not at the bottom.
  4. Three points of substance. Concrete things it does, not adjectives.
  5. Objection handling. The two or three reasons a reasonable person would hesitate, answered directly.
  6. The action again. Same wording, same destination.
", "

That's it. Landing pages get worse as they get longer, almost without exception.

", "

The signup question, answered honestly

", "

", "

What works instead is a link out to something that already handles it:

", "
  • Your email tool's own hosted signup page.

  • Your form tool's hosted form, for anything longer.

", "

Describe the product and the reader. Kodely won't invent statistics, customer counts, testimonials or logos for you — anything factual has to come from you, which is the right way round for a page whose whole job is to be believed.

A landing page for Ledgerly, a bookkeeping tool for solo tradespeople in the UK. The reader is a self-employed electrician who does their books on a Sunday night and hates it. What causes it, what actually works against it, and what no prompt can fix.", "category": "Explainers", "targetKeyword": "ai generated website looks generic", "body": [ "

You described your business, pressed build, and got back something competent and completely forgettable. Hero, three cards, a footer. It's the most common complaint about AI builders and it has a specific cause — mostly fixable, partly not. Here's both halves.

", "

The cause

", "

A language model asked for \"a website for a bakery\" produces the average of every bakery website it has seen. That average is real: it exists, it's competent, and it's the reason your output looks like everyone else's. The model isn't being lazy — you gave it a category, and the average of a category is what a category looks like.

", "

Every specific thing you add pulls the result away from that average. Every vague thing you add pulls it back towards it. That's the whole mechanism, and almost every fix below is an application of it.

", "

Fix one: describe the business, not the website

", "

\"A modern website for a bakery with a hero, three features and a contact section\" briefs a layout. The model is already good at layout. What it can't know is what makes yours specific.

", "

\"A sourdough bakery that sells out by 11am, two loaves done properly plus whatever pastry the baker felt like that morning, regulars order the night before by text\" gives it a scarcity story, a two-product menu, and a texting habit — three things to build a page around that no other bakery page has.

", "

Fix two: name one visual idea, not three moods

", "

\"Modern, clean, professional\" describes nearly every website ever made, so it steers nothing at all. One concrete idea steers everything.

", "

Compare \"editorial, like a printed menu — cream paper, deep ink, serif headings with wide letterspacing, thin rules between sections, one oversized number per price\" against \"clean and modern\". The first has a point of view. The second is a request for the average.

", "

Kodely's builder is asked to give each page one distinctive visual idea rather than a generic hero-plus-three-cards. It can only do that if there's something in your brief to be distinctive about.

", "

Fix three: bring real content

", "

This is the one people skip, and it does more than everything else combined. Generated sites look generic largely because they're full of generic content — and they're full of generic content because the prompt contained none.

", "

Kodely deliberately won't invent facts about a real business: no addresses, no phone numbers, no prices, no opening hours, no testimonials, no statistics. So if you don't supply your actual price list, your actual service names, your actual coverage area, the page has nothing but category-average filler to put there.

", "

A page with your real prices, your real hours and your real service names simply cannot look like anyone else's, because nobody else has those.

", "

Fix four: make round two a subtraction

", "

The instinct after a generic first build is to ask for more. More sections, more features, more copy. That reliably makes it more generic, because you're adding more category-average material.

", "

Cut instead. \"Remove the testimonials section entirely.\" \"Delete the third feature card and make the other two twice the size.\" \"Cut the about paragraph to one sentence.\" A page with three things said properly reads as designed. A page with eight things said adequately reads as generated.

", "

Every successful build is a checkpoint under the History tab, and restoring one is free — it restores a snapshot rather than generating anything. So cutting aggressively costs you nothing if you were wrong.

", "

Fix five: be specific in your edits

", "

\"Make it look better\" gives the model no target, so it produces another average. Compare:

", "
  • Vague: \"the colours are off\". Specific: \"the green is too dark and cold — lighter and warmer, closer to olive\".
  • Vague: \"more modern\". Specific: \"increase the space between sections by half, and make the headings about 30% larger\".
  • Vague: \"needs more personality\". Specific: \"rewrite the hero in the voice of someone who's been doing this for twenty years and isn't trying to impress anyone\".
", "

Use Enhance as a first draft of the brief

", "

If writing a detailed brief is the part you don't want to do, the Enhance button takes a one-liner and expands it into a structured version — audience, goal, tone, sections, key content — which you then edit. Editing a draft is much easier than writing one from nothing, and the edits are where your specifics get in.

", "

Enhance is free and never charged as a build.

", "

What no prompt will fix

", "

Two limits are structural, and no amount of prompting gets around them.

", "

No photography. Published sites can't load anything from another host, so there are no images beyond what the page draws itself in CSS and inline SVG. If your mental image of \"not generic\" is a striking full-bleed photograph, that specific thing isn't available. Why, in full.

", "

No custom fonts. Type comes from the system font stack. A distinctive typeface is one of the fastest routes to a distinctive site, and it's closed here. What's left is scale, weight, spacing and contrast — which is more than it sounds, but it isn't the same lever.

", "

Both of those are consequences of the security policy that makes published sites safe to host, and neither is going to be loosened per-site. The complete list of limits is here.

", "

The short version

", "

Generic in, generic out. Describe the business rather than the layout, name one visual idea, bring your real numbers and copy, and make your second round a subtraction. That gets you most of the way — and the remaining distance is a design constraint you should know about before you start rather than after.

", "

Final state verified: validator clean, seed idempotent, `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` both pass, and only `content/` and `scripts/seo/` are new (nothing else touched). ## What I built **Pipeline** (all under `C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\scripts\seo\`) - `lib.mjs` — dependency-free `.env` loader (never overrides an already-set var), article loader, row mapper. Articles store `body` as an **array of block-level HTML strings**; `bodyHtml` is derived by joining them, so there's one definition of the transform. - `validate.mjs` — 20+ checks, exits non-zero on failure, exports `validateAll()` for reuse. Negative-tested against a deliberately broken fixture: it caught every planted fault (slug/filename mismatch, 84-char title, 5-char meta, bad category, uppercase keyword, non-block body entries, `src=`, absolute URL, ``, `
`, unclosed ``/`
`, `
`, bare `&`, external link, dangling `/blog/` cross-link).
- `seed.mjs` — `--dry-run` prints a field-level diff; refuses to run if any article fails validation; **diffs before writing** so unchanged rows aren't touched (Prisma's `@updatedAt` fires on any `update` call, so an unconditional upsert would churn the column on every deploy); has no delete path at all — rows it doesn't own are printed as "left alone".

Verified against the local DB: 17 created → re-run reports `0 created, 0 updated, 17 unchanged`. I perturbed a row and confirmed the update path detects and repairs exactly the changed fields.

**17 articles** in `content/seo/` (Guides 6, Explainers 7, Comparisons 4 — every category has ≥2 so the related-posts query always has something).

## Two claims I had to retract mid-way — worth flagging

I drafted these as true and then failed to ground them:

1. **"You see an estimated cost range before you spend."** `estimateCredits()` in `lib/credits.ts` is exported but **has zero callers** — nothing in `app/` or `components/` uses it. The estimate is not surfaced in the UI today. Removed from three articles. The "about N builds left" figure *is* real (`averageBuildCredits` → `CreditMeter.tsx`), so that's what the credits article now describes.
2. **"The builder is instructed never to produce a form that pretends to work"** and **"Kodely won't invent your address/prices/testimonials."** Both of those rules live in `ENHANCE_SYSTEM` (`lib/enhance.ts`) — they are **not** in the builder's SYSTEM prompt in `lib/agent.ts`. The builder is in fact told to write *"Real, specific copy… never placeholder headings"*, which pushes it toward inventing an address if you don't supply one. All seven affected articles now say the accurate and more useful thing: there's no backend so a form can't work — *don't ask for one*; and any fact you omit will be filled in with a plausible invention, so bring your real details and proofread before publishing.

Per the brief's own logic that's arguably a product gap worth closing: adding the enhance-style "invent no facts about a real business" and "never a form that works" rules to `lib/agent.ts`'s SYSTEM would make the honest version of these articles considerably stronger.

Grouped by what would have to ship first.
